your-program-and-the-memory-map.title: Your program and the memory map
your-program-and-the-memory-map.description: Think of a program as a house with rooms for different kinds of work. Run this tiny program, then find the value that belongs to the house and the value…
your-program-and-the-memory-map.html:
Think of a program as a house with rooms for different kinds of work. Run this tiny program, then find the value that belongs to the house and the value used by one call.

  • Find global and local on the stage and say where each one lives
  • Say why local is gone after main returns, but global is not
  • Name the package and function where every Go program starts

variables.title: Variables
variables.description: A variable is a labeled drawer. Change what is inside it, then open a smaller room with another drawer carrying the same label.
variables.html:
A variable is a labeled drawer. Change what is inside it, then open a smaller room with another drawer carrying the same label.

  • Predict both printed values when an inner block declares x again
  • Explain the difference between x := 20 and x = 20 inside a block
  • Spot shadowing: two different variables that share one name

types-sizes-and-numbers.title: Types, sizes and numbers
types-sizes-and-numbers.description: A sized integer is like a small wheel with a fixed number of positions. Turn it past its last position and compare that runtime behavior with an overflowing…
types-sizes-and-numbers.html:
A sized integer is like a small wheel with a fixed number of positions. Turn it past its last position and compare that runtime behavior with an overflowing constant.

  • Predict what n++ does to an int8 that already holds 127
  • Say why 7/2 prints 3 when both numbers are integers
  • Pick an integer type big enough for the values you need

constants.title: Constants
constants.description: A constant is a value written in the plan, not a drawer you can refill. Predict the numbered labels before running the example.
constants.html:
A constant is a value written in the plan, not a drawer you can refill. Predict the numbered labels before running the example.

  • Predict the value iota gives each name in a const group
  • Explain why green and blue need no = iota of their own
  • Say why &red is a compile error

control-flow.title: Control flow
control-flow.description: A loop is a route that visits the same place again. Follow the instruction marker rather than assuming every line is visited just once.
control-flow.html:
A loop is a route that visits the same place again. Follow the instruction marker rather than assuming every line is visited just once.

  • Trace i and sum through each turn of the loop
  • Say which value of i is skipped and why the total is 8
  • Explain the difference between continue and break

functions-and-the-call-stack.title: Functions and the call stack
functions-and-the-call-stack.description: Calling a function is like handing a copy of a worksheet to someone else. Let the helper change its copy, then check the original sheet.
functions-and-the-call-stack.html:
Calling a function is like handing a copy of a worksheet to someone else. Let the helper change its copy, then check the original sheet.

  • Point to the two separate x slots: one in main, one in change
  • Say why main still prints 7 after change sets its x to 99
  • Send a result back to the caller with a return value

pointers.title: Pointers
pointers.description: A pointer is an address tag attached to a drawer. Follow the tag to change the original value, rather than making another copy of the number.
pointers.html:
A pointer is an address tag attached to a drawer. Follow the tag to change the original value, rather than making another copy of the number.

  • Follow the arrow from p to x and say what it means
  • Explain why x prints 42 though the code never assigns to x directly
  • Say what &x does and what *p does

arrays-and-structs-layout.title: Arrays and structs: layout
arrays-and-structs-layout.description: A struct is a parcel with named compartments. Reorder the compartments and measure the spaces between them before deciding which parcel is smaller.
arrays-and-structs-layout.html:
A struct is a parcel with named compartments. Reorder the compartments and measure the spaces between them before deciding which parcel is smaller.

  • Say why a byte plus an int64 takes 16 bytes, not 9
  • Predict how adding or reordering fields changes a struct's size
  • Explain why assigning an array or struct copies all of it

strings.title: Strings
strings.description: Text is a row of encoded tiles, and a visible character can occupy several tiles. Count bytes and then walk the decoded runes to see the difference.
strings.html:
Text is a row of encoded tiles, and a visible character can occupy several tiles. Count bytes and then walk the decoded runes to see the difference.

  • Say why len("héllo") is 6 when you can see only 5 letters
  • Explain why the range loop skips byte offset 2
  • Count characters with len([]rune(s)) instead of len(s)

slices.title: Slices
slices.description: Two slices can be two windows into one room. Change a value through one window and look through the other before checking the output.
slices.html:
Two slices can be two windows into one room. Change a value through one window and look through the other before checking the output.

  • Point to the one backing array that both a and b reach
  • Explain why writing b[0] changes what a prints
  • Make a slice with its own storage using make and copy

append-and-growth.title: Append and growth
append-and-growth.description: Appending is like adding one more item to a shelf. If the shelf has room, its neighbors may see the change; otherwise the items need another shelf.
append-and-growth.html:
Appending is like adding one more item to a shelf. If the shelf has room, its neighbors may see the change; otherwise the items need another shelf.

  • Predict whether append reuses a's array or makes a new one
  • Explain why b[0] = 9 also shows up in a here
  • Use len and cap to tell whether an append has room

maps.title: Maps
maps.description: A map is a lookup desk: you ask for a key rather than a position. Ask for a missing key, then use the extra result to distinguish absence from a stored zero.
maps.html:
A map is a lookup desk: you ask for a key rather than a position. Ask for a missing key, then use the extra result to distinguish absence from a stored zero.

  • Say why both lookups print 0
  • Use the ok value to tell a stored zero from a missing key
  • Predict what reading a missing key from a nil map returns

copy-or-share.title: Copy or share?
copy-or-share.description: Copying a value can be like copying a parcel or copying a window’s address card. Compare an array copy with a slice copy before deciding which changes travel.
copy-or-share.html:
Copying a value can be like copying a parcel or copying a window’s address card. Compare an array copy with a slice copy before deciding which changes travel.

  • Say why b[0] = 8 leaves a alone
  • Say why t[1] = 9 does change a
  • Look at a value and ask: does it hold the data, or point to it?

methods-receivers-and-embedding.title: Methods, receivers and embedding
methods-receivers-and-embedding.description: A method receiver is another worksheet handed to a function. Compare changing the worksheet copy with following a pointer back to the original counter.
methods-receivers-and-embedding.html:
A method receiver is another worksheet handed to a function. Compare changing the worksheet copy with following a pointer back to the original counter.

  • Say why CopyTick does not change c.N
  • Explain what the * in (c *Counter) changes
  • Choose a pointer receiver when a method must update its value

closures.title: Closures
closures.description: A closure is a helper that remembers where a shared notebook lives. Call two helpers and see whether they keep separate copies or write in the same notebook.
closures.html:
A closure is a helper that remembers where a shared notebook lives. Call two helpers and see whether they keep separate copies or write in the same notebook.

  • Explain why the last a() prints 12, not 2
  • Point to the single n that both closures write to
  • Give a closure its own variable so it stops sharing

interfaces.title: Interfaces
interfaces.description: An interface is a labeled container that remembers what kind of thing it carries. Compare an empty container with one carrying a typed nil pointer.
interfaces.html:
An interface is a labeled container that remembers what kind of thing it carries. Compare an empty container with one carrying a typed nil pointer.

  • Say why value == nil is false though p is nil
  • Name the two parts an interface value carries: a type and a value
  • Write an interface variable that really is nil

nil-one-word-six-meanings.title: Nil: one word, six meanings
nil-one-word-six-meanings.description: Nil is a family of empty containers, not one universal operation. Pick a container kind and test what an operation is allowed to do with it.
nil-one-word-six-meanings.html:
Nil is a family of empty containers, not one universal operation. Pick a container kind and test what an operation is allowed to do with it.

  • Predict len of a nil slice and of a nil map
  • Say why reading a missing key from a nil map is safe
  • Name one thing you cannot do with a nil map

errors.title: Errors
errors.description: Wrapping an error is like placing a note inside another envelope. Add context without losing the original note, then search the chain for that cause.
errors.html:
Wrapping an error is like placing a note inside another envelope. Add context without losing the original note, then search the chain for that cause.

  • Say what %w keeps that %v throws away
  • Explain what errors.Is searches for
  • Add context to an error without hiding its cause

defer-panic-and-recover.title: Defer, panic and recover
defer-panic-and-recover.description: Deferred calls are cleanup notes stacked beside a function. Watch the newest note run first, then follow the notes when a panic unwinds the call.
defer-panic-and-recover.html:
Deferred calls are cleanup notes stacked beside a function. Watch the newest note run first, then follow the notes when a panic unwinds the call.

  • Predict the order in which deferred calls run
  • Explain why saved prints 1 though n is 2 at the end
  • Use a closure in defer to read a value at exit time

generics.title: Generics
generics.description: A type parameter is a blank label on a reusable tool. The constraint says which materials the tool can work on before anyone calls it.
generics.html:
A type parameter is a blank label on a reusable tool. The constraint says which materials the tool can work on before anyone calls it.

  • Say which types ~int | ~int64 allows T to be
  • Explain how Go picks T in Add(2, 3) without being told
  • Extend the constraint so Add also works with float64
